Population.evidence_source: [/page/3/Text/10] Ten participants, 25–65 years of age, were recruited into this study. All had been in very close familial relationships with the deceased persons and were bereaved for between 2 and 20 years (see Table 1). All decedents were male, 20–60 years of age, and hanging was the most common form of suicide (n = 6).

Area.evidence_source: [/page/3/Text/13] one of the participants reported that the decedents had a prior history of mental health or substance abuse issues (see Table 2). [/page/3/Text/14] Although many had moved on in the sense that they were re-partnered, and able to function well in various aspects of their lives, all still experienced a deep sense of loss and continued to express their grief, sadness, and regret over the events surrounding the suicides. Their desire to contribute something positive was such that several participants were actively engaged in volunteer and activism works in the area of suicide bereavement and mental health support. Furthermore, a number of participants indicated that they considered their participation in this study to be a way that they could help others through sharing their experiences. [/page/3/Text/15] Thematic analysis revealed three key themes. These are: (1) He Tried to Hang Himself: Purposeful indications of the intent to end life; (2) They Still Ignored It: Disappointment with health services; and (3) Nobody Talked to Me: Exclusion of family members from treatment information.
